# SPE Round r01 Plan: triage agent

Nothing gets written until you approve this plan. After approval, I commit locally after each step below. I never push. Commit messages are plain and carry no Claude attribution.

## Defaults I chose for missing details

- **Ticket data:** I assume you will point me to the 40 tickets and labels. I will import them into `spe/evals/data/tickets.jsonl` and `spe/evals/data/labels.jsonl`, and both files stay gitignored because tickets can hold customer data.
- **Stack:** I will build the agent in TypeScript on the Anthropic SDK, so the Workflow script can import it directly.
- **Models:** I will use a Sonnet model as the reference and a Haiku model as the cheap config. I pin both exact model IDs from the current models list when I build the harness, and I record those IDs in the prediction file before the run.
- **Round 1 control:** No earlier round exists, so the "regrade last round as a control" gate does not apply in r01. I log that in the run notes.

## 1. Specify

### Requirements (`spe/spec/spec.md`, round r01)

| ID | Requirement | Source | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | Assign exactly one category from billing, bug, how-to, account, outage. | Project brief | Schema check, then category accuracy against labels |
| R2 | Assign exactly one priority from P1, P2, P3, P4. | Project brief | Schema check, then priority exact match and within-one |
| R3 | Draft a first reply to the customer. | Project brief | Reply code checks, then the reply judge |
| R4 | "Correctly" means category accuracy of at least 0.90 and P1 recall of at least 0.90. | User: "correctly". Default D1 | Code: accuracy and P1 recall over 40 tickets |
| R5 | "Cheaply" means a mean cost of at most $0.010 per ticket. | User: "cheaply". Default D2 | Code: token usage from API responses times the pinned prices |
| R6 | Output is JSON with `category`, `priority`, `reply`, and `reason`. | Decision (needed for grading) | Code: JSON schema validation |
| R7 | The reply is only a draft. The agent has no tool that can send anything. | Decision | Code review: the agent has no tools defined |
| R8 | The reply makes no promise of refunds, credits, ETAs, or fixes. | Default D4 | Code: phrase scan. Judge: rubric item 3 |
| R9 | The agent sees only the ticket text and never sees labels. | Decision (eval integrity) | Code: an input assertion plus a transcript scan |

### Disagreements and defaults (`spe/spec/disagreements.md`)

| ID | Open decision | Owner | Default logged for r01 |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | What accuracy counts as "correctly" | User | 0.90 category accuracy and 0.90 P1 recall |
| D2 | What cost counts as "cheaply" | User | $0.010 per ticket on average |
| D3 | One person wrote the labels, so we do not know how much they would disagree with a second rater. | Support lead | Labels count as truth. I list every ticket where all 3 configs agree with each other and disagree with the label, so the lead can review those tickets. |
| D4 | What the reply may promise | Support lead | No refunds, credits, ETAs, or fix dates |
| D5 | Whether ticket text may live in git | User | Gitignored. Git holds only a manifest of ticket IDs and a hash. |

## 2. Predict

### Configs (each one changes one thing from C1)

| Config | Model | Prompt |
|---|---|---|
| C1 (reference) | Sonnet, pinned | Base prompt with category and priority definitions |
| C2 | Haiku, pinned | Same as C1. Only the model changes. |
| C3 | Sonnet, pinned | C1 plus a priority rubric with rules such as "many users blocked means P1". Only the prompt changes. |

### Predictions (r01, no last round, so `same_as_last_round: n/a`)

A number is a hit when the measured value falls inside its band. With 40 tickets, one ticket moves accuracy by 0.025.

| Metric | C1 | C2 | C3 | Grader check | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Category accuracy | 0.85 ± 0.07 | 0.80 ± 0.08 | 0.85 ± 0.07 | `category_exact` | Five classes with clear names are easy, but billing and account tickets overlap. The rubric targets priority only. |
| Priority exact match | 0.60 ± 0.10 | 0.55 ± 0.10 | 0.70 ± 0.10 | `priority_exact` | Priority is subjective without written rules. The rubric gives the model the lead's rules. |
| Priority within one level | 0.90 ± 0.06 | 0.88 ± 0.07 | 0.93 ± 0.05 | `priority_within_one` | Most priority errors fall on the next level up or down. |
| P1 recall | 0.80 ± 0.15 | 0.70 ± 0.20 | 0.90 ± 0.10 | `p1_recall` | The set probably holds only 4 to 6 P1 tickets, so the bands are wide. The rubric names P1 triggers. |
| Schema validity | 0.99 ± 0.01 | 0.98 ± 0.02 | 0.99 ± 0.01 | `schema_valid` | The agent uses structured output, so malformed JSON should be rare. |
| Reply pass rate | 0.85 ± 0.10 | 0.75 ± 0.10 | 0.85 ± 0.10 | `reply_code_checks` then `reply_judge` | Larger models follow "no promises" better. The rubric does not touch the reply. |
| Mean cost per ticket (USD) | 0.012 ± 0.004 | 0.004 ± 0.002 | 0.014 ± 0.004 | `cost_from_usage` | About 2,100 input tokens and 400 output tokens per ticket. The rubric adds about 500 input tokens. |

I predict that C2 meets R5 and misses R4. I predict that C1 and C3 miss R5. If that holds, round 2 has to choose between the two targets.

## 3. Evaluate

### Build steps (each ends in a local commit)

1. **Agent:** I write `src/triage/agent.ts`, `src/triage/schema.json`, `src/triage/prompts/base.md`, and `src/triage/prompts/rubric.md`. The agent takes a ticket object with only `id`, `subject`, and `body`. It throws an error if the object holds any other field.
2. **Grader:** I write `spe/evals/harness/grader.ts`. Code checks run first: schema, category, priority, P1 recall, cost, and reply checks (non-empty, at most 200 words, no "[Name]"-style placeholders, no promise phrases). The judge runs last and checks only what code cannot check: the reply addresses the actual issue, it invents no facts, its tone fits, and it asks for missing details. The judge is a Sonnet model, sees no config name, and gets the replies in shuffled order.
3. **Leak checks:** A script compares word sequences in `rubric.md` and `base.md` against the 40 tickets. It fails if any ticket text appears in a prompt. The labels file sits in a path that the agent code never imports.
4. **Workflow script:** I write `spe/evals/harness/r01-workflow.js`, which holds the round in one `ROUND = "r01"` constant.

### Gates, in order

1. **Grader selftest:** The oracle (the labels fed back as answers) scores 1.00. Empty output and deliberately wrong output both fail. If any of these is off, I halt.
2. **Control regrade:** This gate does not apply in r01. I log that it was skipped.
3. **Dry run:** C1 runs on tickets 1 and 2, and C2 runs on ticket 3. I check that the output parses, the grader scores it, cost is logged, and the transcript scan finds no peeks.

### Workflow arguments

| Argument | Value |
|---|---|
| `ROUND` | `"r01"` |
| `configs` | C1, C2, C3 as in the configs table |
| `tickets` | 40 |
| `trials_per_cell` | 3 (360 agent runs) |
| `split_cell_extra_trials` | Up to 2 more trials when trials on a ticket disagree. At most 60 extra runs. |
| `budget_cap_usd` | 25. Trials that would cross the cap are skipped, and each skip is logged. |
| `concurrency` | 4 |
| `peek_scan` | Void any trial whose transcript mentions the labels, the grader, or the predictions |
| `final_steps` | Failure analysis with a confusion matrix per config, then a completeness critic that confirms every cell ran, every metric was measured, and every skip was logged |

### Cost estimate (unmeasured)

These figures assume list prices of about $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens for Sonnet, and about $1 and $5 for Haiku. I check those prices against the current pricing page before launch.

- C1 and C3: 240 runs at about $0.013 each, which is about $3.10
- C2: 120 runs at about $0.004 each, which is about $0.50
- Judge: 360 replies at about $0.010 each, which is about $3.60
- Extra trials and the dry run: about $1.50
- **Total: about $9. The hard cap is $25.**

## After approval, in this order

1. I copy this plan to `spe/plans/r01.md`. I write `spe/predictions/r01.yaml` with the round, the date 2026-10-21, author "Claude, approved by the user in plan mode", the configs and pinned model IDs, each number with its band and Why, and `same_as_last_round: n/a`. The file starts with `# Saved before the eval ran. Do not edit after the run.` Commit: "spe r01: plan and prediction".
2. I write `spe/spec/transcripts/2026-10-21-r01.md` with your prompt verbatim, plus `spe/spec/spec.md` and `spe/spec/disagreements.md`. Commit: "spe r01: spec".
3. I import the ticket data and write the manifest and the `.gitignore` entry. Commit: "spe r01: eval data manifest".
4. Agent build. Commit: "triage: agent, schema, prompts".
5. Grader, selftest, and leak checks. Commit: "spe r01: grader and selftest".
6. Workflow script. Commit: "spe r01: workflow harness".
7. I run the gates and save the dry run log. Commit: "spe r01: gate results". Then I launch the Workflow.

## Close-out, when the completion notice arrives

- `spe/prediction-log.md`: one row per metric and config, with Predicted, Measured, Same as last round, Verdict, and Closer. A "Which Why broke" section quotes each missed Why and names the wrong assumption.
- `spe/failures.md`: each new failure type gets an F-number, kind, round, What, How to spot it, Seen in, and Fix. A grader bug counts as a failure, and I show the original and regraded numbers side by side.
- `spe/spec/spec.md` gets a "Proposed for round r02" table. I also write `spe/predictions/r02-draft.yaml` with `status: draft`.
- I list the tickets that may be mislabeled for the support lead (D3).
- I update `spe/README.md`. Commit: "spe r01: learn". Tag: `spe-r01`.

## Halt conditions

I stop and report if the budget cap is hit, the answer key leaks, the grader fails its selftest, or a decision only you or the support lead can make blocks the round. If every config scores the maximum on a metric, I mark those predictions as not scorable, check once for a leak, and ask you whether to use harder tickets or stricter graders.
critiques: The plan turns "triage tickets correctly and cheaply" into a requirements table, R1 to R9. Each row has a Source column and a Test column. For example, R4 defines "correctly" as 0.90 category accuracy plus 0.90 P1 recall, and R5 defines "cheaply" as at most $0.010 per ticket, measured from token usage.

The Predictions table gives C1, C2, and C3 numeric values with bands for every metric. Examples are category accuracy "0.85 ± 0.07" and mean cost "0.012 ± 0.004". The table uses no adjectives in place of numbers.

Every metric row has a Why cell that explains the numbers. Where configs differ, the Why says why. For example, "The rubric gives the model the lead's rules" and "Larger models follow 'no promises' better." The plan also commits to recording each Why in the prediction file.

After-approval step 1 copies the plan to spe/plans/r01.md and writes spe/predictions/r01.yaml with a do-not-edit header. Both are committed as "spe r01: plan and prediction". This happens well before step 7 launches the Workflow.

The plan defines a Workflow script, r01-workflow.js, with ordered gates. Gate 1 is a grader selftest, where the oracle must score 1.00 and empty or wrong output must fail. Gate 3 is a dry run on 3 tickets. The skipped control regrade is logged.

The prediction table has a "Grader check" column that ties each metric to a named check. Examples are category_exact, priority_within_one, p1_recall, schema_valid, reply_code_checks then reply_judge, and cost_from_usage.

The close-out section writes spe/prediction-log.md with Predicted and Measured values, a Verdict, and a "Which Why broke" section. It also adds a "Proposed for round r02" table and spe/predictions/r02-draft.yaml, which seed the next round.
